title: Interfaces
summary: An **interface** is a set of method signatures — a behavioral contract. In Go a type satisfies an interface **implicitly** (structural typing): just by having the right methods, with no `implements` keyword. Under the hood an interface value is a **two-word (type, value) pair**, which is the key to understanding dynamic dispatch and the famous nil-interface gotcha.

subtopics.title: Implicit satisfaction (structural typing)
subtopics.explanation: A type satisfies an interface simply by having all of its methods — there is no `implements` keyword and no explicit declaration. The compiler checks the method set at the point of assignment. This decouples the type from the interface, so you can satisfy interfaces you don't even know exist.
subtopics.example:
type Stringer interface{ String() string }
// any type with String() string already satisfies it

subtopics.title: The (type, value) two-word representation
subtopics.explanation: An interface value holds two words: a pointer to a type descriptor (the dynamic type) and a pointer to the underlying value (or the value itself). When you call a method, Go uses the type descriptor to dispatch to the right implementation. This pair is why nil handling is subtle.
subtopics.example: var w io.Writer = os.Stdout // type=*os.File, value=stdout

subtopics.title: The empty interface: interface{} / any
subtopics.explanation: interface{} has no methods, so EVERY type satisfies it — it can hold any value. Since Go 1.18, `any` is a built-in alias for interface{}. Use it sparingly: you lose static type information and must type-assert or type-switch to get it back.
subtopics.example: var x any = 42; x = "now a string" // both fine

subtopics.title: Accept interfaces, return concrete types
subtopics.explanation: Define small interfaces at the CONSUMER (the function that uses the behavior), not at the producer. Functions should accept interfaces to stay flexible, but return concrete types so callers keep full information. io.Reader, io.Writer, fmt.Stringer and error are the canonical small interfaces.
subtopics.example: func Save(w io.Writer, data []byte) error // accepts any writer

subtopics.title: Method sets decide satisfaction
subtopics.explanation: If a method has a POINTER receiver, only *T is in the method set, so only *T satisfies the interface — a plain T value does not. Value-receiver methods are in both T and *T's method sets. This ties directly back to the methods topic.
subtopics.example: func (c *Counter) Inc() {} // only *Counter satisfies an Incer

subtopics.title: The nil-interface gotcha
subtopics.explanation: An interface is nil ONLY when BOTH its type and value are nil. Storing a nil *T into an interface makes the interface NON-nil, because it now carries a type. This causes the classic bug where a function returns a typed-nil error and `if err != nil` is unexpectedly true.
subtopics.example: var p *MyErr = nil; var e error = p; e == nil // false!

foundations.overview: An interface describes WHAT a type can do, not what it is. It lists method signatures — a contract of behavior — and any type that has those methods satisfies it automatically, with no inheritance and no `implements` keyword. This implicit, structural approach is one of Go's defining design choices: it lets you write functions against small behavioral contracts (like io.Reader) and pass in any type that fits, even types written long after the interface.
foundations.formalDefinition: An interface type is a named set of method signatures. A value of concrete type T implements interface I if T's method set includes every method of I; an interface value is a (dynamic type, dynamic value) pair that dispatches method calls to the underlying concrete type.
foundations.whyItMatters: Interfaces are how Go achieves polymorphism and decoupling without classes or inheritance. They power the standard library (io, fmt, sort, error), enable testable code via dependency injection, and are one of the most-probed Go interview topics — especially the (type, value) representation and the nil-interface trap.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an interface as a job posting that lists required skills (methods). Any candidate (type) with those skills can take the job — no diploma or family tree (inheritance) required. The interface value is like a badge that records both who the candidate is (the dynamic type) and a way to reach them (the value), so the right person answers when you call.
foundations.runtimePerspective: An interface value is two machine words: an itable/type pointer and a data pointer. For non-empty interfaces the first word points to an itab (interface table) caching the concrete type plus its method pointers; the empty interface stores the type pointer directly. A method call reads the itab to find the function pointer and jumps to it — that is dynamic dispatch. The data word holds the value or a pointer to it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: io.Reader/io.Writer abstract files, sockets, and buffers behind one contract; error is an interface so any type can be an error; sort.Interface lets one algorithm sort any collection; database/sql and http handlers are defined in terms of interfaces so implementations are swappable.
foundations.businessImpact: Coding to small interfaces lets teams swap implementations (real vs. mock, one vendor vs. another) without rewrites, shortening delivery time and reducing the cost of change as systems evolve.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Interfaces enable dependency injection and isolated unit tests: pass a fake that satisfies the interface. Defining interfaces at the consumer keeps packages loosely coupled and avoids import cycles.
foundations.performanceImpact: An interface method call is an indirect (dynamic) dispatch, slightly slower than a direct call and not inlinable. Storing a value in an interface can also cause a heap allocation (boxing). On hot paths, prefer concrete types or generics; elsewhere the cost is negligible.
commonUseCases: Dependency injection and mocking in tests
Defining error as a behavioral contract

commonMisconceptions.myth: A type must declare that it implements an interface.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Satisfaction is implicit and structural — if the methods match, the type satisfies the interface automatically, with no `implements` keyword.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An interface holding a nil pointer equals nil.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It does NOT. An interface is nil only when both its type and value are nil; a typed nil pointer gives the interface a type, so it is non-nil.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interfaces are like classes / give you inheritance.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are behavioral contracts, not types you subclass. Go favors composition; an interface only says what methods a value must have.

visualExplorer.title: Inside an interface value
visualExplorer.caption: An interface value is two words: a type descriptor (the dynamic type) and a pointer to the underlying value. Method calls dispatch through the type descriptor — and an interface is nil only when BOTH words are nil.

visualExplorer.title: How a method call dispatches
visualExplorer.caption: What happens when you call a method on an interface value.

config.intro: From assignment to dynamic dispatch, step by step:

steps.name: Assign concrete to interface
steps.detail: `var w io.Writer = f` records f's dynamic type (*os.File) in word one and a pointer to f in word two.

steps.name: Build/lookup the itab
steps.detail: The runtime finds or builds an interface table mapping io.Writer's methods to *os.File's actual function pointers.

steps.name: Call through the interface
steps.detail: `w.Write(p)` reads the itab to find the concrete Write and the data word for the receiver.

steps.name: Dynamic dispatch
steps.detail: Control jumps to *os.File's Write — the correct implementation is chosen at runtime, not compile time.

steps.name: nil check
steps.detail: `w == nil` is true only if both words are nil; a typed-nil pointer leaves word one set, so w != nil.

interactiveExamples.title: One interface, two concrete types
interactiveExamples.explanation: Both Dog and Cat have a Speak() method, so both satisfy Speaker with no `implements` keyword. The announce function accepts the interface and works for either type — that's implicit satisfaction plus dynamic dispatch.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the type satisfy fmt.Stringer
interactiveExamples.explanation: fmt.Stringer is satisfied by any type with `String() string`, and fmt uses it automatically when printing. Add the method so Println prints the friendly form instead of the struct fields.

checkpoints.explanation: get() returns a *MyErr that is nil, but assigning it to the error interface gives the interface a non-nil TYPE (*MyErr) with a nil value. An interface is nil only when both type and value are nil, so the comparison is false. This is the classic typed-nil bug.

checkpoints.prompt: A method on Counter uses a pointer receiver: func (c *Counter) Inc(). Which satisfies an interface Incer{ Inc() }?
checkpoints.explanation: Pointer-receiver methods are in the method set of *Counter only, not of the value type Counter. So only *Counter satisfies Incer. (Value-receiver methods would be in both method sets.)

checkpoints.prompt: This is meant to print the value, but it won't compile. Why?
options: You can't do arithmetic on an interface value; assert/switch to the concrete type first
Value() must use a pointer receiver
checkpoints.explanation: num is an interface value, not an int — interfaces only expose their methods, not the underlying type's operators. To do arithmetic you must recover the concrete value, e.g. num.Value() + 1, or type-assert num.(N).v + 1.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the empty-interface type so this function accepts a value of ANY type.
checkpoints.explanation: The empty interface accepts any type. Since Go 1.18 the built-in alias `any` is preferred over the equivalent `interface{}`. `interface` and `struct{}` are not valid here, and `var` is a keyword, not a type.

codeLab.title: Polymorphic area with an interface
codeLab.instructions: Define `Shape` with `Area() float64`, implement it for `Rectangle{W, H}` and `Circle{R}`, and write `Solve(shapes []Shape) float64` that returns the total area. Use math.Pi for the circle.
hints: Shape needs exactly one method: Area() float64. Any type with that method satisfies it implicitly.
Give Rectangle and Circle value-receiver Area() methods so both T and *T satisfy Shape.
In Solve, range over the slice and accumulate s.Area() — the call dispatches to the real type.

debuggingLab.title: The error that is never nil
debuggingLab.symptom: The function returns no error, yet the caller's `if err != nil` block always runs.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: This compiles and runs — it is a LOGIC bug, not a compile error. query returns `err`, a *DBError that is nil, but the declared return type is the `error` INTERFACE. Assigning a typed nil pointer to an interface stores a non-nil dynamic type (*DBError) alongside a nil value, and an interface is nil only when BOTH its type and value are nil. So `err != nil` is unexpectedly true even though the pointer was nil.
commonMistakes: Returning a concrete pointer type (*DBError) from a function declared to return `error` and relying on it being nil.
Declaring the error variable as a concrete pointer type instead of `error`.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make query return a true nil interface on the happy path by using the `error` type directly and returning a plain `nil`.

theory.question: What is an interface in Go and how does a type satisfy it?
theory.directAnswer: An interface is a set of method signatures — a behavioral contract. A type satisfies it implicitly (structurally): if the type's method set contains every method the interface lists, it satisfies the interface automatically, with no `implements` keyword or explicit declaration. The compiler verifies this at the assignment site.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A named set of method signatures that describes behavior, not data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give Go polymorphism and decoupling without classes or inheritance, so functions depend on behavior rather than concrete types.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: At assignment the compiler checks the concrete type's method set against the interface; at runtime an interface value holds a (type, value) pair and dispatches calls through a method table (itab).

theory.whyImportant: Implicit satisfaction is a defining feature of Go and underpins the standard library (io, fmt, error); it's a near-guaranteed interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: *os.File and *bytes.Buffer both satisfy io.Writer simply by having Write([]byte) (int, error), so fmt.Fprintf works with either without them knowing about io.Writer.

followUps.question: Where should you define an interface?
followUps.answer: At the consumer — the package that USES the behavior — not the producer. Accept interfaces, return concrete types.

followUps.question: What is the empty interface?
followUps.answer: interface{} (alias `any` since Go 1.18) has no methods, so every type satisfies it; it holds any value but loses static typing.

theory.question: Why can an interface value be non-nil even when it holds a nil pointer?
theory.directAnswer: Because an interface value is a (type, value) pair, and it equals nil only when BOTH the type and the value are nil. Storing a nil *T into an interface records *T as the dynamic type, so the type word is non-nil — making the interface non-nil even though the underlying pointer is nil.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The typed-nil interface trap: an interface carrying a concrete type but a nil value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Interfaces must record the dynamic type to support method dispatch, so a typed nil still carries that type.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: `var p *T = nil; var i I = p` sets the type word to *T and the data word to nil; `i == nil` compares both words and is false.

theory.whyImportant: It causes the classic bug where a function returning a concrete pointer as `error` is wrongly treated as an error — a favourite interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A function declared to return error returns a *MyError that happens to be nil; callers' `if err != nil` fires incorrectly, signalling a failure that never happened.

followUps.question: How do you avoid it?
followUps.answer: Return the `error` interface directly and return a plain `nil` on success, rather than a concrete typed nil pointer.

followUps.question: How can you detect it at runtime?
followUps.answer: Use reflection (reflect.ValueOf(i).IsNil()) after a type assertion, but the real fix is not to produce typed nils in the first place.

scenario.question: Your team wants unit tests that don't hit the real database. How do interfaces let you do this cleanly?
scenario.directAnswer: Define a small interface at the consumer describing only the methods your code uses (e.g. UserStore{ GetUser(id) (User, error) }). Your production code depends on that interface, not the concrete DB type. In tests, pass a fake struct that satisfies the interface and returns canned data. Because satisfaction is implicit, the fake needs no relationship to the real store.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Dependency injection through a consumer-defined interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Interfaces decouple a caller from a concrete implementation, so the implementation can be swapped for a fake.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The function accepts the interface; tests inject a mock satisfying it; production injects the real type — both selected at call time.

scenario.whyImportant: Decoupling via small interfaces is the backbone of testable, maintainable Go services.
scenario.realWorldExample: A handler takes a UserStore interface; tests pass an in-memory fake, while main wires in the Postgres-backed implementation.

followUps.question: Should the interface be big or small?
followUps.answer: Small — list only the methods the consumer actually calls. Large interfaces are hard to fake and couple you to many methods.

followUps.question: Where do you put the interface definition?
followUps.answer: In the consumer package, so the producer doesn't need to import or know about it (avoids import cycles).

coding.question: Implement `func Describe(vals []any) []string` that returns a string for each value: ints as "int:N", strings as "str:S", and "other" for anything else.
coding.thoughtProcess: The input is []any (empty interface), so each element's concrete type is unknown statically. Recover it with a type switch — the idiomatic way to branch on the dynamic type of an interface value. Pre-size the result slice for efficiency, and build the formatted string per case.
coding.lineByLine: We pre-size out to len(vals). The `switch x := v.(type)` form is a type switch: in each case, x is already the concrete type, so we can use it directly (x as int, x as string). The default branch handles any other dynamic type. We append a formatted string per element and return the slice.

followUps.question: What's the difference between a type switch and a type assertion?
followUps.answer: A type assertion v.(T) checks one type (use the comma-ok form to avoid a panic); a type switch branches over several possible dynamic types at once.

followUps.question: Why use the comma-ok form v, ok := i.(T)?
followUps.answer: Without ok, a failed assertion panics; with ok you get the zero value and ok=false, letting you handle the mismatch safely.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define small interfaces at the consumer and accept them as parameters; return concrete types. This keeps packages decoupled, avoids import cycles, and lets implementations evolve independently. Resist 'header interfaces' that mirror a whole struct — they add coupling, not flexibility.
productionDeepDive.performance: Interface method calls are dynamic dispatch (an indirect jump that can't be inlined), and boxing a value into an interface may allocate on the heap. On hot paths prefer concrete types or generics; reserve interfaces for boundaries where flexibility matters.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: An interface value itself is just two words, but whether it's safe to use concurrently depends entirely on the concrete type behind it. Document and synchronize the underlying implementation; an interface gives no thread-safety guarantees.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Beware the typed-nil interface trap when returning errors: return the `error` interface and a plain nil on success. Use the comma-ok type assertion to avoid panics when recovering concrete types from interface values.
productionDeepDive.observability: When logging or wrapping errors, prefer errors.Is/errors.As over type assertions so wrapped error chains are inspected correctly. Logging an interface value prints its dynamic type with %T, useful for diagnosing typed-nil and dispatch surprises.
productionDeepDive.security: Avoid passing untrusted data around as `any` and asserting blindly — a wrong assertion panics. Validate the dynamic type with the comma-ok form, and don't let interface indirection hide where unvalidated input flows.

caseStudies.problem: Code needed to work with files, network sockets, and in-memory buffers uniformly.
caseStudies.solution: Define tiny interfaces — io.Reader and io.Writer (one method each) — that everything implements implicitly.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Dynamic dispatch costs a little speed, but the decoupling is enormous.
caseStudies.lessons: Small, single-method interfaces compose into a powerful, swappable ecosystem.

caseStudies.problem: Support many database drivers without the core package knowing about each one.
caseStudies.solution: Define driver behavior as interfaces; each driver implements them and registers itself.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Indirection and some reflection, but vendor-neutral and extensible.
caseStudies.lessons: Interfaces at the boundary let third parties plug in without touching core code.

keyTakeaways: An interface is a set of method signatures; a type satisfies it implicitly (structurally) just by having those methods — no `implements` keyword.
An interface value is a two-word (type, value) pair, which is why method calls dispatch dynamically and why nil handling is subtle.
An interface is nil only when BOTH its type and value are nil; a typed nil pointer makes the interface non-nil — the classic error-return bug.
Favor small interfaces (io.Reader, error), define them at the consumer, accept interfaces and return concrete types; recover concrete types with type assertions/switches.
